title: The Puppet Who Cut Her Strings
summary: A wooden puppet named Sela wakes one night to find she is alive, and the first thing she does is cut the strings that let her master move her. But free of the strings, she cannot move at all — and must learn that the strings were never only a leash, and that true freedom is not having no strings, but choosing your own.

chapters.title: The Night She Woke
chapters.body:
Sela was a marionette — a wooden puppet with painted eyes and jointed limbs, hung from four strings that ran up to a wooden control-cross, worked by the hands of the old puppeteer who had carved her. For years she had known nothing, felt nothing, been nothing but wood and string, dancing when the puppeteer moved her, still when he set her down. And then, one night, in the dark of the puppeteer's workshop, hanging on her hooks among the other still puppets, Sela woke up.

She became aware. Alive. She felt the wood of her own body, and the four strings running up from her limbs, and a mind — her own mind — blinking awake behind her painted eyes. She could think. She could feel. She was, suddenly and astonishingly, someone.

And the very first thing Sela felt, waking into life as a puppet on strings, was outrage at the strings.

Because she understood at once what they were. Four strings, running up from her hands and her knees to the control-cross, by which the puppeteer moved her — made her walk, made her dance, made her bow, made her do whatever he wished. She was a thing on strings, controlled, moved about at another's will, with no say in where she went or what she did. And now that she was alive, now that she had her own mind and her own wishes, the strings seemed intolerable. A leash. A set of chains. The very symbol of her not being free. How could she be a real, living, free person with strings running up from her limbs to a cross that someone else controlled?

So Sela, in her first hour of life, filled with the fierce desire to be free, did the thing that seemed most obviously right: she reached up with her newly-alive wooden hands, and she found the strings, and one by one, she cut them. Snip. Snip. Snip. Snip. All four strings, severed, falling loose. No more control-cross. No more puppeteer's hands. No more being moved about at another's will. She had freed herself. She was, she thought triumphantly, free at last — a living puppet with no strings, beholden to no one, master of herself.

And then she tried to take a step, to walk out into her new free life.

And she collapsed in a heap on the workshop floor.

Because she could not move. Not at all. Her wooden limbs, alive now, full of her own will and her own wishes — would not obey her. She wanted to lift her arm, and it did not lift. She wanted to stand, and she could not stand. She lay in a tangled heap of jointed wood, alive and aware and full of desire to move, and completely unable to, because the strings were gone. And Sela understood, with a dawning horror, that she had made a terrible mistake — though she did not yet understand what it was.

chapters.title: Free and Unable to Move
chapters.body:
Sela lay on the workshop floor for the rest of that night, a heap of living wood, unable to move a single limb, and she thought hard about what had gone wrong.

She had cut the strings to be free. And she was free — free of the puppeteer, free of the control-cross, free of being moved about at another's will. But she was also, now, unable to move at all, because — she slowly understood — the strings had never been only a leash. The strings were also how a puppet's limbs moved. They were the connection between will and motion, the thing that let intention become movement. When the puppeteer had held them, yes, his will had moved her. But the strings themselves were not the problem — they were the very means of moving. And she had cut them all, and so she had cut away not just the puppeteer's control, but her own ability to move at all. She had thrown out the thing that made motion possible, along with the thing that made her motion someone else's.

When the old puppeteer came into his workshop the next morning and found Sela alive — a puppet blinking and speaking and thinking on his floor — he was astonished, but he was also, being old and wise, not entirely surprised, as if he had half expected that one of his creations might someday wake. And when Sela, in her distress, explained what she'd done — woken up, wanted to be free, cut her strings, and now could not move — the old puppeteer sat down beside her on the floor, and nodded slowly, and did not laugh at her, though there was a deep old sadness and kindness in his eyes.

"Ah, little one," he said. "You did what nearly every newly-freed thing does. You thought the strings were your chains, and cut them all, and found you'd cut away your own legs. It's the oldest mistake there is." He picked up the four cut strings, gently. "The strings were never only my control of you. They were also how you move — the connection between what a puppet wills and what a puppet does. When I held them, I moved you, yes. But the answer to that was never to cut the strings. It was to take hold of them yourself."

Sela did not understand, and said so.

"Freedom," the old puppeteer said, "is not having no strings. A thing with no strings can't move at all — it just lies where it falls, free and helpless, unable to do anything it wishes. That's not freedom; that's just being cut loose, which is a different thing entirely. Real freedom, little one, is not the absence of strings. It's holding your own strings. It's being the one whose hand is on the control-cross of your own life — so that your limbs still move, still dance, still walk, but they move by your will, toward your wishes, under your own control." He held up the cut strings. "You didn't need to cut these. You needed to take them out of my hands and put them into your own. The mistake was thinking the strings themselves were the problem. The strings were only a problem because someone else was holding them. Held by you — chosen by you, worked by you — those same strings are exactly what set you free."

And Sela began to understand. She had thought freedom meant no strings, no connections, no control of any kind — and had cut herself into a helpless heap. But the puppeteer was telling her that freedom wasn't the absence of the strings. It was the ownership of them. Not being uncontrolled, but being self-controlled. Not having nothing move her, but being the one who moves herself.

chapters.title: The Strings She Chose
chapters.body:
The old puppeteer offered to help Sela, and what he offered was not what she had first wanted, but what she truly needed.

He could not un-cut the strings she'd severed — but he could give her new ones, and, more importantly, he could teach her to hold them herself. Carefully, gently, he attached new strings to Sela's living limbs — to her hands, her knees — and he ran them up not to a control-cross held by his hands, but to small holds that Sela herself could grasp, with her own wooden fingers. And then he taught her, patiently, over many days, how to work them. How to move her own arm by pulling her own string. How to make her own leg step by guiding her own thread. How to be, at last, the puppeteer of herself.

It was hard, and it was slow. Moving yourself by your own strings, it turned out, was far more difficult than being moved by someone else's hands. When the puppeteer had worked her strings, Sela had danced gracefully, effortlessly — because he was skilled, and she had only to hang there and be moved. Now, working her own strings, she was clumsy, and she stumbled, and her movements were awkward and halting, because she was learning to control herself, and self-control is a difficult art that no one is good at right away. There were times she missed the old ease of being moved by another — times when holding her own strings felt so much harder than simply hanging limp and letting someone else do it. But she understood, now, the difference. Being moved gracefully by another was not freedom, however easy it was. Moving herself clumsily, by her own will, was freedom, however hard.

And slowly, Sela got better at it. Day by day, she learned to work her own strings more skillfully — to walk, then to walk smoothly; to move, then to move gracefully; to become, bit by bit, the master of her own motion. And the movements she made were hers now. When she walked, she walked where she wanted to go. When she danced, she danced the dance she chose. She was still a puppet on strings — she would always be a puppet on strings, for that was what she was — but the strings ran up to her own hands now, and that changed everything. She was free, not because she had no strings, but because she held her own.

And she understood, at last, the whole of the thing. She had woken up believing that freedom meant cutting every string, throwing off all control, being beholden to nothing and no one. And that belief had left her a helpless heap on the floor, free and unable to move. Because that kind of freedom — the absence of all strings, all connections, all control — is not freedom at all. It's just being cut loose, helpless, unable to act on any of your wishes. Real freedom is harder and better than that. Real freedom is holding your own strings: being connected, yes, being moved, yes, but by your own hand, toward your own wishes, under your own control. It's not the absence of the strings that make you move. It's being the one who moves them.

Sela lived a long life after that, as a living puppet who held her own strings — and she was free, truly free, in the only way anyone ever is. Not free of all connection and control, which is only helplessness. But free to move herself, by her own will, toward her own chosen life. She even danced in the old puppeteer's shows sometimes, when she wanted to — but now she chose the dance, and worked her own strings, and it was her performance, freely given, not a thing done to her. And when other newly-woken things came to her — other puppets, other freshly-alive creatures, filled with the fierce first desire to cut every string and be free of all control — she taught them what the old puppeteer had taught her: that cutting your strings does not make you free, it makes you helpless. That freedom is not having no strings. It's holding your own. And that the hardest and truest freedom of all is not to be uncontrolled, but to become, clumsily and slowly and at last skillfully, the master of yourself — the one whose own hand is on the strings of your own life.
